title: Readers’ Rides: Nate’s Mostly Forever Hardtail – Chasing That Feeling, Mostly Forever – Nathan Cain & Julia Sparks
content:
For this week’s Readers’ Rides, we have a fun article written by Julia and Nate from Chariot Bike in Bend, Oregon. Read on for the story behind Nate’s Mostly Forever hardtail!

I recently commissioned Max Keegan (of Mostly Forever bikes) to build a custom titanium hardtail – something simple, capable, and built to take me anywhere I set out to explore. What I got was a snappy, poppy, playful bike that continues to impress me every time I get out for a ride. The bike climbs gracefully and encourages long days in the saddle. When I point it downhill, it comes alive and demands more speed through every corner. What surprises me most is how forgiving it feels through the trail chunk and chatter. After getting more familiar with my new ride, I stopped noticing the bike altogether and found myself just flying through the forest on a beautiful machine built for 6 foot 8 me.

Long before MF bikes existed, before the titanium frames, and precision welds, before the evenings spent building bikes after a workday at a fabrication shop, Max was simply a kid riding a BMX bike downhill near his childhood home. He’s been chasing that feeling ever since. “I’ve wanted to build bikes since mostly forever,” he says.

If you walk into Max’s workspace expecting to hear about titanium tubes, geometry charts, or the latest bike industry trends, instead you’ll probably end up talking about long rides, humbling experiences, and why bicycles mattered in the first place. I sent over some questions to gain some additional insight into Mostly Forever.

What first made you want to build bicycles instead of simply riding them?

I grew up riding freestyle BMX and continued that well into my 30s. The idea to build bikes was formed by BMX companies like FBM, S&M, and Solid bikes, in conjunction with the exposure to shop classes in junior high and high school.

Why did you start with steel and what drew you to titanium?

Steel is approachable in both cost and forgiveness. You can join steel bike frames with multiple processes i.e. brazing, TIG welding, or even torch welding. Titanium though? Not so much. I was drawn to titanium when I was asked to add some bottle bosses to a titanium frame; I was blown away by how light the frame was when it was handed to me. Beyond the weight reduction, what really drew me in was the corrosion resistance and finishing options. I’ve ridden a lot of raw steel bikes. I love a well-patina-laden frame, but we all know that decreases the lifespan. With titanium I can leave it raw, letting my imperfections be acknowledged. My work isn’t hidden under a layer of paint, it’s out in the open, it’s vulnerable.

Do you remember the first frame you ever built? What would you change if you saw it today?

I was at a crossroads when I decided to build my first frame. For the first time in my life I had the skill-set, a work-space, and a welder. I could buy a custom frame or I could invest in myself and the tools to make my own. The first was made with a minimum amount of tooling: hacksaw and hand-files, wooden tubing blocks, and a vice. I purchased an inexpensive frame fixture off eBay from a builder in Tucson (Heeler Cycles) and bought the machined parts from Paragon. I wouldn’t change anything about that first one!

What qualities do you chase more than anything—comfort, speed, handling, durability, liveliness?

When a person is comfortable they are able to express themselves. For me, riding is an expression. When you are comfortable on a bike all the qualities of the design can be tapped into.

Are there any trends in the bike industry that you intentionally ignore?

I try to ignore the bike industry in general. I am fatigued from a lifetime of marketing and the bike industry has a lot of that happening. Oh and drop bars, when will that trend disappear :)

Is there a tool in your shop you couldn’t live without?

I could live without all of it, but if I want to be open for business and continue to grow, I should acquire more tools.

How does being a rider influence your frame building?

I think it’s paramount to be a rider first and a designer/builder second. Anyone who spends or has spent a great deal of time riding bikes realizes how adaptable we are as humans. Bike design can only take you so far, physical fitness and bike-handling skills are going to have a greater impact on your riding than the bike you are on. You can ride most any bike most anywhere, and if you can’t pedal, start pushing.

What kind of terrain inspires your designs?

I love riding my bike on single track in the backcountry and riding all the roads necessary to get there.

What are you currently obsessed with improving?

My process – from the design communications with the customer to the movements I make in the shop. I learn something every time I do any part of the process; there’s a lifetime of refinement ahead.

What separates a good frame from an exceptional one?

The differences are subtle, like finishing work, quality of materials, or the tolerances the builder adheres to. I make good frames; Brad Bingham makes exceptional frames. He’s got a process and a skill set that far exceeds my current capabilities. We could build two identical-geometry bikes and they would both ride nearly identically, the differences aren’t simply what you can see when they are sitting next to each other.

Where do you see custom frame building in ten years?

Oofffda. No idea. What’s life going to be like next year? I’m not heavily invested in the future, it’s overwhelming to think about. Human existence is not guaranteed.

What’s your favorite ride in Oregon?

I certainly havent ridden them all, nor will I ever, but I try to enjoy the one I’m on. Favorite routes in Oregon would be the Oakridge Ultracruze and the Oregon Timber Trail.

If you could build a bike for anyone—past or present—who would it be?

My mother. She was never a cyclist, but we rode bikes together when I was a kid. I’d love to go for a ride with her again.

Living in Bend, Oregon reshaped the way Max rides. BMX taught him creativity and expression. Central Oregon’s endless singletrack and forest roads gave that expression somewhere to grow. His ideal ride isn’t necessarily technical or extreme. It’s simply following dirt as far as it goes. His current titanium hardtails reflect that preference, but his curiosity is drifting toward bikes built for dirt touring and longer adventures.

The name Mostly Forever doesn’t refer to durability. Bikes that are ridden hard eventually wear out. They’re supposed to. The name is partially a nod to MF DOOM and a WU-Tang reference, and part refusal to take branding too seriously. “You’ve got to call it something” Max says, and that attitude carries into nearly every part of his work.

When I ask Max what he hopes someone would say while riding one of his bikes twenty years from now, it’s not that it’s fast, nor that it’s rare, or even that it’s beautiful. “I hope they say, I’m glad to be alive, and it’s pretty cool that I can get out and ride this thing’.” Maybe that’s Mostly Forever in a single sentence. Not performance. Not legacy. Instead, simply gratitude for another ride. And maybe that’s what Max Keegan has been building all along. Not just titanium frames, but opportunities to rediscover that familiar feeling we all had as kids; coasting down a hill with nowhere to be except exactly where the bike was taking us.
